raw_case_text: A 64-year-old male developed severely disseminated KS five months after ABO-incompatible kidney-transplantation. The patient had end-stage renal disease due to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and was on peritoneal dialysis for eight months prior to transplantation. Per protocol, the patient was treated with a single dose rituximab (375 mg/m2) and intravenous (i.v.) immunoglobulin therapy (IVIG) before transplantation and induction therapy was i.v. basiliximab and methylprednisolone (MP). Posttransplantation immunosuppression consisted of prednisolone, tacrolimus (Tac), and mycophenolatemofetil (MMF). One week after transplantation, the patient was treated for borderline rejection with three days of i.v. MP (250 mg/day). At discharge, serum creatinine was 1.6 mg/dl and immunosuppression was tapered in the outpatient clinic. Five months after transplantation, the patient developed purple-red elements on the skin of the forehead, nose, and penis. Two months after presentation of skin elements, the patient was admitted and enlarged lymph nodes in both groins were found. Biopsies from both skin and lymph nodes revealed KS with tumour growth through the capsule of the lymph node. A Positron Emission Tomography CT (PET-CT) revealed pathologically enlarged and metabolically active lymph nodes in the mediastinum, left side of the retroperitoneum, and both groins as seen in Figure 1(a). The patient tested positive for HHV-8 and negative for HIV. Ten cycles of paclitaxel (30 mg) and gemcitabine (304 mg) were given on days 1 and 8, with hemodialysis performed the following two days after chemotherapy to remove metabolites of gemcitabine. Paclitaxel and gemcitabine doses were increased over the treatment period to a final dose of 138 mg (approximately 80 mg/m2) and 1416 mg (approximately 800 mg/m2), respectively. Immunosuppression was initially changed by discontinuing MMF and switching from Tac to everolimus (Eve). Due to the severity of the disease Eve was also stopped and prednisolone 5 mg/day was given as monotherapy. Throughout the treatment period, the patient had great variation in creatinine due to infections and urinary tract obstruction with creatinine ranging between 1.7 and 6.2 mg/dl. PET-CT performed after courses 4 and 6 and 8 showed regression of all lymph node enlargements and complete remission of KS after course 10. Hemodialysis was discontinued after termination of chemotherapy and the patient then maintained a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dl. A PET-CT 15 months later showed continuous complete remission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old male presented 5 months after ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation with purple-red cutaneous lesions on his forehead, nose, and glans penis, followed 2 months later by bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having undergone ABO-incompatible living-donor kidney transplantation 5 months earlier (with pre-transplant rituximab 375 mg/m2 and IVIG, basiliximab/methylprednisolone induction, triple maintenance with prednisolone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil, and a 3-day methylprednisolone pulse at week 1 for borderline rejection), the patient developed violaceous-red skin lesions on his forehead, nose, and penis at 5 months post-transplant, progressing over the next 2 months to bilateral inguinal lymph node enlargement.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), on peritoneal dialysis for 8 months prior to ABO-incompatible renal transplantation 5 months earlier; borderline acute allograft rejection 1 week post-transplant.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for violaceous skin nodules on the forehead, nose, and penis and bilateral inguinal swelling. Post-transplant immunosuppressive medications: prednisolone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil.

objective.physical_examination: Purple-red cutaneous papules/plaques on the forehead, nose, and penis, accompanied 2 months later by bilateral enlarged inguinal lymph nodes.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline post-transplant serum creatinine was 1.6 mg/dL (fluctuating between 1.7 and 6.2 mg/dL during chemotherapy due to UTIs and urinary obstruction before returning to 1.6 mg/dL). HHV-8 testing was positive and HIV testing was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin and inguinal lymph node biopsies confirmed Kaposi sarcoma with extracapsular nodal tumor extension. Whole-body FDG PET-CT demonstrated pathologically enlarged, hypermetabolic mediastinal, left retroperitoneal, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe disseminated mucocutaneous and nodal post-transplant iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8-positive, HIV-negative) developing 5 months after ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation. Management consisted of stepwise immunosuppression reduction (discontinuing mycophenolate mofetil, switching tacrolimus to everolimus, and subsequently stopping everolimus to maintain prednisolone 5 mg/day monotherapy) combined with 10 cycles of systemic paclitaxel (escalated from 30 mg to 138 mg [~80 mg/m2] on days 1 and 8) and gemcitabine (escalated from 304 mg to 1,416 mg [~800 mg/m2] on days 1 and 8, followed by 2 days of post-infusion hemodialysis to clear gemcitabine metabolites). Serial PET-CT scans after courses 4, 6, 8, and 10 and at 15 months post-chemotherapy confirmed complete metabolic and clinical remission with preserved renal allograft function off dialysis (creatinine 1.6 mg/dL).
